title: The structure of the atom
summary: Learn what is inside an atom: protons, neutrons, electrons and how they are arranged.
cards.0.p: An atom is made of three particles. The proton has a charge of +1, the neutron has no charge, and the electron has a charge of −1. A proton and a neutron each have a mass of about 1 amu. An electron is 1836 times lighter than a proton.
cards.0.key: The charges of a proton and an electron are equal in size but opposite in sign. amu stands for atomic mass unit.
cards.1.p: The nucleus, where the protons and neutrons are, is 10 000 to 100 000 times smaller than the atom, but more than 99.9% of the mass is there.
cards.1.svg#2: The atom's diameter is ~10⁴–10⁵ times the nucleus's
cards.1.key: The rest of the atom is the empty space where the electrons are.
cards.2.p: The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number (Z), and it decides what the atom is. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, and every atom with 8 protons is oxygen.
cards.2.key: Z = number of protons (in a neutral atom, the number of electrons is also Z)
cards.3.p: The total number of protons and neutrons is the mass number (A). A is written at the upper left of the symbol, and Z at the lower left. For example, the atom 2311Na has 12 neutrons.
cards.3.key: Since A = p + n, the number of neutrons is A − Z.
cards.3.once.soru: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. About how many amu is its mass?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: A proton and a neutron are each about 1 amu, and electrons have almost no mass. So 6 + 8 = 14. This number is called the mass number.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: 6 is only what the protons add. Each neutron also adds about 1 amu.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: You counted only the neutrons. Each proton also adds 1 amu.
cards.4.p: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Their chemical properties are the same, but properties that depend on mass, such as density, are different.
cards.4.key: Neutral isotopes also have the same number of electrons. The isotopes of hydrogen are <sup>1</sup>H, <sup>2</sup>H (deuterium) and <sup>3</sup>H (tritium).
cards.5.p: An atom that gives up or gains electrons becomes an ion. An atom that gives up electrons becomes a positive cation (Na+), and an atom that gains electrons becomes a negative anion (Cl−). The number of protons does not change.
cards.5.key: The charge of an ion is the number of protons minus the number of electrons.
cards.6.p: Atoms with the same number of neutrons are called isotones (¹⁴C, ¹⁶O). Atoms with the same mass number are called isobars (¹⁴C, ¹⁴N). These atoms belong to different elements.
cards.6.etk.soru: Match each pair of particles with the right name, based on the number they share.
cards.6.svg#12: only isotopes are the same element
cards.6.key: Atoms with the same number of protons are isotopes. Only isotopes belong to the same element.
cards.6.once.soru: What do the atoms ¹⁴C and ¹⁶O have in common? (C: 6, O: 8 protons)
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons, and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. Atoms with the same number of neutrons are called isotones.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Carbon has 6 protons and oxygen 8. If they had the same number of protons, they would be the same element.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The mass numbers are written at the upper left of the symbol, and they are 14 and 16.
cards.7.p: Particles with the same number of electrons are called isoelectronic. To count, start from the neutral atom. For a cation, subtract as many electrons as its charge. For an anion, add as many electrons as its charge.
cards.7.svg#10: number of electrons = Z − ion charge
cards.7.key: Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Ne, F⁻ and O²⁻ all have 10 electrons.
cards.7.once.soru: How many electrons does the Na⁺ ion have? (Na: 11 protons)
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Neutral sodium has 11 electrons. The + charge shows that sodium gave up one electron, so 11 − 1 = 10. The Ne atom also has 10 electrons.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: 11 is the number of electrons in neutral sodium. Think about what the + charge tells you.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: A cation is a particle that gives up electrons, not one that gains them.
cards.8.p: The atomic mass in the periodic table is an average based on how common each isotope is in nature. That is why it is not a whole number.
cards.8.svg#3: atomic mass in the table = average by abundance
cards.8.svg#4: mass number (A): p + n count of a single atom
cards.8.key: The mass number is always a whole number. The average atomic mass can be a decimal.
cards.8.once.soru: 75% of chlorine atoms are ³⁵Cl and 25% are ³⁷Cl. What is the average atomic mass of chlorine?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The more common isotope counts more. 0.75 · 35 + 0.25 · 37 = 35.5.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: 36 is the plain average of the two masses. But ³⁵Cl is three times more common.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The average comes out close to the more common isotope. Check which one is more common.
cards.9.p: Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus. For the first 20 elements, the 1st shell holds at most 2 electrons, and the 2nd and 3rd shells hold at most 8 each.
cards.9.key: Na (11 electrons) is arranged 2-8-1, and Ca (20 electrons) 2-8-8-2. You will see why the 3rd shell stops at 8 in the topic on modern atomic theory.
cards.10.p: The electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons. Atoms tend to complete their outer shell to 8 (2 for the very small ones), like the noble gases (gases such as He, Ne and Ar that do not react).
cards.10.key: That is why Na gives up 1 electron and Cl gains 1 electron.
cards.11.p:
• Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus, and electrons are around it.
• Z is the number of protons, and A is the total number of protons and neutrons.
• Isotopes share Z, isotones share the number of neutrons, isobars share A, and isoelectronic particles share the number of electrons.
• An ion is an atom that has gained or given up electrons.
• For the first 20 elements, shells fill as 2-8-8.
quiz.0.q: Magnesium has atomic number 12. How many electrons are in the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion?
quiz.0.e: A neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons. After giving up 2 electrons, 12 − 2 = 10 electrons are left.
quiz.1.q: Put each pair of atoms in the right group. (Z: H 1, He 2, C 6, N 7, O 8, Na 11, Mg 12, Ar 18, Ca 20)
quiz.1.e: Isotopes share the number of protons, and isobars share the mass number. Isotones share the number of neutrons. <sup>13</sup>C and <sup>14</sup>N have 7 neutrons, and <sup>23</sup>Na and <sup>24</sup>Mg have 12.
quiz.2.q: Use the counters to build the <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> ion. (Cl: Z = 17)
quiz.2.e: Since Z = 17, the atom has 17 protons. The number of neutrons is A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20. The charge is −1, so there is one extra electron, giving 18 electrons.
quiz.3.q: In nature, 20% of boron atoms are <sup>10</sup>B and 80% are <sup>11</sup>B. What is the average atomic mass of boron, approximately?
quiz.3.e: The average is weighted by abundance. 0.20 · 10 + 0.80 · 11 = 2 + 8.8 = 10.8. The heavier isotope is more common, so the result is close to 11.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Build an atom yourself by adding and removing particles.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The atom on the screen is helium. Its nucleus has 2 protons and 2 neutrons, and there are 2 electrons around it.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Where is almost all of the atom's mass?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Protons and neutrons have similar masses. An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton. So almost all of the mass is in the nucleus.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The shells make up the atom's volume, but electrons are very light. A proton has about the mass of 1836 electrons.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: An electron is much lighter than a proton. Where does the weight collect?
A:adimlar.1.metin: An atom is so small that 3 million of them side by side make only 1 millimeter. Now you will zoom into a lithium atom.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: If you blew an atom up to the size of a football stadium, how big would the nucleus in the middle be?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: About the size of a pea
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The nucleus's diameter is about 100 000 times smaller than the atom's. In a stadium-sized atom, the nucleus would be a pea in the middle of the field.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: About the size of a soccer ball
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Even a soccer ball is far too big.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The nucleus is only a tiny dot inside the atom.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Add particles from the tray below. Tap a particle in the atom to remove it. Turn hydrogen into a neutral carbon atom and look at the element's name.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: 6 protons make carbon. The number of protons decides the element. One more proton and it would be nitrogen. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
A:adimlar.3.metin: This is a carbon atom. Add neutrons to its nucleus and see whether the element changes. Make the mass number (A) 14.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: The atom is still carbon, because it has 6 protons. But A = 6 + 8 = 14. Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Carbon-14 is used to find the age of ancient remains.
A:adimlar.4.metin: This is a sodium atom. Tap one of its electrons to remove it.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The atom has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so its charge is 11 − 10 = +1. The nucleus did not change at all. Becoming an ion only changes the number of electrons.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Change the number of protons and see how the electrons are arranged in shells.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a chlorine atom (17 protons)?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The 17 electrons are arranged 2-8-7. The 7 electrons in the outer shell are why chlorine tends to gain one electron and become Cl⁻.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: First the first two shells fill, holding 2 + 8 = 10 electrons. How many electrons are left: 17 − 10?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Set the number of protons to 17 and count the shells.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Now build everything yourself. Make sulfur with mass number 32 that has gained two electrons, the ³²S²⁻ ion. Set the number of protons first.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: 16 protons make sulfur, and the number of neutrons is 32 − 16 = 16. A neutral atom would have 16 electrons. After gaining 2 electrons it has 18, and the charge is 16 − 18 = −2.
A:kapanis.0: An atom is made of a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. The ¹H nucleus has no neutrons. The mass is in the nucleus, and the volume is mostly empty space.
A:kapanis.1: The number of protons is the atomic number (Z), and it decides the element.
A:kapanis.2: The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.
A:kapanis.3: The charge is the number of protons minus the number of electrons. An atom that gives up electrons becomes a cation, and one that gains electrons becomes an anion.
A:kapanis.4: For the first 20 elements, shells hold at most 2, 8 and 8 electrons. The rest go to the 4th shell, so the Ca atom is arranged 2-8-8-2.
